title: Diagonalisability: When A = P D P^-1
quickIdea: A is diagonalisable exactly when it has n linearly independent eigenvectors; put them in the columns of P and the eigenvalues on the diagonal of D.
remember: A is diagonalisable if and only if it has n linearly independent eigenvectors, that is, if and only if GM = AM for every eigenvalue.
n distinct eigenvalues are enough, because eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are independent; they are not necessary.
With A = P D P^-1, every power is A^k = P D^k P^-1, which is why diagonalisation makes powers cheap.
A real symmetric matrix is always diagonalisable, and orthogonally so: A = Q Lambda Q^T with Q orthogonal.
Similar matrices P^-1 A P have the same characteristic polynomial, hence the same eigenvalues, trace and determinant.

example.answer: A = P diag(3,1) P^-1 with P = [[1,1],[1,-1]]. The two eigenvalues are distinct, so independence was guaranteed before any computation.

gateAngle: 2018 Q.26 is this card in one line: if every eigenvector lies on a single line, the matrix has fewer than n independent eigenvectors, so it cannot be diagonalised and its eigenvalue must repeat. The option that also claims it has no inverse is the trap, because a matrix can be non-diagonalisable and still invertible.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Is A = [[1,2],[0,1]] diagonalisable?
variations.why: det(A - lambda I) = (1-lambda)^2 gives AM = 2, while A - I = [[0,2],[0,0]] has rank 1 so GM = 1. With only one eigenvector direction there is no invertible P.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why do n distinct eigenvalues guarantee n independent eigenvectors?
variations.answer: If c1 v1 + ... + ck vk = 0 were a shortest dependence among eigenvectors of distinct eigenvalues, applying A gives c1 lambda1 v1 + ... + ck lambdak vk = 0, and subtracting lambda_k times the first relation leaves a shorter dependence, which is impossible.
variations.why: This is the standard induction argument, and it is why the distinct case never needs the AM = GM test.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A is 3x3 with eigenvalues 1, 1 and 2, and rank(A - I) = 1. Is A diagonalisable?
variations.why: GM(1) = 3 - 1 = 2 = AM(1), and the eigenvalue 2 has AM = GM = 1, so there are three independent eigenvectors in total.

trap.what: Thinking a repeated eigenvalue blocks diagonalisation, or that a non-diagonalisable matrix must be singular.
trap.why: Diagonalisability is about having enough independent eigenvectors, which is independent of whether the determinant is zero.
trap.counterexample: A = [[2,1],[0,2]] is not diagonalisable and yet det A = 4, so it is invertible. Conversely [[2,0],[0,2]] has the same repeated eigenvalue and is already diagonal.

check.question: A is 2x2 with eigenvalues 4 and 4, and A is not a multiple of the identity. Is A diagonalisable?
check.explanation: A 2x2 with a double eigenvalue 4 either is 4I, which is diagonal, or has A - 4I of rank 1, giving GM = 1 against AM = 2. Since A is not 4I, it is defective.
